references.text: God declares that He blots out transgressions for His own sake—a foundational Old Testament text about God's forgiveness of sins, which Jesus here claims to exercise.

Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven and whose sin is covered. David pronounces blessed the one whom the Lord forgives—this is the background for Jesus' words on the forgiveness of sins.
"He who forgives all your iniquity"—the Psalm praises God as the One who forgives sins, which Jesus here does as the Son of Man.
The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus sees their faith and says to the paralytic: "Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven."
The parallel passage in Mark where Jesus sees their faith and says to the paralytic: "Son, your sins are forgiven."
Jesus says to the woman who anointed His feet: "Your sins are forgiven"—a similar situation where Jesus declares forgiveness of sins.
Jesus confirms His authority to forgive sins by healing the paralytic, showing that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.
Paul preaches in Antioch that forgiveness of sins is proclaimed through Jesus—the apostles' proclamation of the very forgiveness that Jesus Himself practiced.
God made us alive with Christ and forgave us all our trespasses—Paul links the forgiveness of sins to Christ's work.
The prayer of faith will save the sick, and if he has committed sins, they will be forgiven him—the connection between faith, healing, and forgiveness of sins.
Without faith it is impossible to please God—Jesus sees their faith and acts on it, underscoring the central role of faith.
Jesus says to the woman: "Your faith has saved you; go in peace"—again, faith and forgiveness are directly linked, as in Luke 5:20.
